2927d60cc3:
This chapter covers everything outside your code that changes what a Claude application does:

  • CLAUDE.md files, treated as reviewed configuration;
  • Claude Code settings.json, with its scopes, precedence, permission rules, env and hooks blocks;
  • model identifiers, and how to pin them through a model's lifecycle;
  • prompts that are versioned, evaluated and rolled out like code;
  • plugin dependencies with semantic-version constraints.

The goal is to get from "it worked yesterday" to a reproducible tuple you can diff.
dca348d5a6:
Neighbouring chapters: chapter 04 owns the application lifecycle and eval strategy in general. Chapter 09 owns what a plugin bundles, marketplaces and install scopes. Chapter 11 owns day-to-day Claude Code operation, including how the CLAUDE.md hierarchy is discovered and loaded. Chapter 15 owns model trade-offs and prompt caching. Chapter 20 owns hook mechanics.

This chapter owns the configuration view. Which file or version holds a behaviour? Who may change it? How is a change reviewed, rolled out and reverted?
bf9bcdac47: Verified against code.claude.com (settings, permissions, model configuration, plugin manifest and dependency pages) and platform.claude.com (model IDs and versions, deprecations) on 2026-10-09. Claude Code changes weekly. Anything marked "check the docs" was not confirmed.
42a81f4944:
The objective names five nouns: CLAUDE.md, settings.json, model version pinning, prompt versioning and plugin dependencies. They look like five unrelated files. In fact they answer one operational question: when behaviour changes, can you say which input changed, who changed it, and how to put it back?

A Spring team answers that for code with git, Maven coordinates and profiles. An LLM team needs the same answer for inputs the compiler never sees. Tests written as exact-match assertions don't catch changes to them either.
38d6923f38:
At 4.1% of 53 items, expect two or three questions on this objective directly. More will show up in debugging and Claude Code questions that borrow from it. Typical stems:

  • "behaviour changed and nothing was deployed"
  • "every developer should get the same permission rules"
  • "a developer must not be able to turn off the guard"
  • "the new model release broke JSON parsing"
  • "the prompt change improved the average but support tickets about porting doubled"
  • "a plugin stopped working after its dependency updated"

The wrong options add words to a prompt or ask people to be careful. The right ones move the requirement to a versioned, enforced, evaluated layer.
56ddee096c: None of these practices is new. Each one is an older software discipline applied to an input that used to be invisible. The lineage helps on the exam, because distractors usually propose the habit from before the discipline existed.
e332ca2b9e:
Around 2011 the twelve-factor guidance said: keep configuration that varies by deployment out of code, in the environment or in files the deployment supplies, and never commit secrets. Spring Boot's application.yml, its profiles and its property-source precedence list (command-line arguments over profile files over defaults) are the Java form of the same idea.

Claude Code's settings files follow the same shape. There are several sources and a documented precedence. Personal files stay out of version control. An organisation-level source sits above everything.

If you know why Spring puts --server.port above application.yml, you already understand why --settings sits above .claude/settings.json.
ca9a68465e:
Maven made version coordinates explicit. Lock files (npm, Poetry, Gradle) made transitive resolution reproducible. The lesson from LATEST and floating ranges was that a build that resolves differently on Tuesday is not the same build.

Hosted model APIs brought the floating dependency back. Early on, a request named a model family and the provider decided which weights answered. Anthropic's IDs have since moved from dated snapshots with convenience aliases (for example claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 and the alias claude-haiku-4-5) to dateless IDs. From the 4.6 generation on, those dateless IDs are themselves fixed snapshots.

Tools built on top, Claude Code included, kept their own moving aliases such as opus and sonnet. Pinning is the same discipline as pinning a Maven version.
492c7227d6:
Teams first kept prompts as string literals. Then they moved them into spreadsheets or vendor consoles, where anyone could edit them in production. The failures were predictable: an untracked edit, no way to say which wording produced last week's outputs, no review.

The response borrowed database-migration habits (Flyway, Liquibase). Every change is a numbered, immutable version with a changelog. The runtime records which version it ran. Rollback means pointing back to a prior version, not editing text in place. Evals took the role of the test suite, because you can't judge a prompt change by whether it compiles.
ced029fbbf:
When coding agents arrived, project conventions moved from wikis into files the agent reads (CLAUDE.md). That made conventions executable, in a loose sense. It also made them a supply-chain input: every session will confidently run a wrong build command in CLAUDE.md.

Agents also needed hard limits the model can't talk its way around. That's why Claude Code separates text the model reads from settings its own code enforces.

Plugins then added packaged extensions with versions. Later they gained declared dependencies on other plugins with semantic-version ranges, and npm-style resolution came along with its conflict cases.
beb93ad249: A workable definition: anything that can change the model's output, or what the agent is permitted to do, without a code change. The definition is broad on purpose. The incident you end up debugging is usually caused by an input nobody thought of as configuration: a teammate's personal CLAUDE.md, a plugin auto-update, a prompt edited in a registry UI, or a Claude Code alias that started resolving to a newer model.
1bde11a146:
Two properties set these inputs apart from ordinary code.

First, they are not checked by a compiler. A misspelled permission rule may only produce a startup warning. A prompt edit is valid text whatever it says. A model swap type-checks. The checks are evals, validators and linters that you build.

Second, some are read by the model and some by the harness. CLAUDE.md, rules files, Skills and prompts are text in the context window, and the model follows them most of the time. Permission rules, hooks, managed settings, model IDs and plugin enablement are applied by code, and they hold every time. Every placement question on the exam comes down to that split.
3977fbe998:
The practical output of configuration management is one log record per model call that names every element of the tuple:

  • the requested model ID;
  • the model field the response reports;
  • the prompt bundle ID, version and content hash;
  • the tool schema version;
  • for Claude Code automation, the settings sources loaded (/status shows them interactively).

With that record, "it changed on Tuesday" becomes a diff between two records rather than a debate. Without it, every investigation starts by guessing.
62e6af7bec: 15_repro_tuple.py in the companion diffs two days of such records and reports which element moved. Note that it logs both model_requested and model_served. They differ when an alias resolves, when a gateway rewrites the ID, or when a fallback model answered.
4ddeba522a:
CLAUDE.md is a Markdown file that Claude Code loads into context at session start. It is not parsed into settings. It is text the model reads every turn, so it acts like a system prompt you keep in git.

Chapter 11 covers how the hierarchy of user, project, directory and managed files is discovered, along with imports, .claude/rules/ path scoping and /memory. This section treats the file as configuration: what belongs in it, which scope owns each line, and how a change is reviewed.
58594d49e5:
The cost model decides the content. You pay for every line in every session, in tokens and in attention. A 600-line CLAUDE.md dilutes the 20 lines that matter. Conflicting lines (one file says Gradle, another says Maven) leave the model to pick.

The test for a line is: would a competent engineer new to this repo get this wrong without being told, on most tasks? If yes, it belongs.

  • If it matters only for some files, it belongs in a path-scoped rule.
  • If it is a procedure used occasionally, it belongs in a Skill loaded on demand.
  • If it must hold every time, it belongs in settings or a hook. CLAUDE.md may mention it, but only so the model plans around it.
93410fb859:
That file holds five configuration faults:

  • The secret is committed, and it is also sent to the model provider on every session.
  • Two "never" rules are enforcement written as text. They hold most of the time, which is not the requirement.
  • The two build commands conflict, so behaviour depends on which one the model weighs more.
  • The runbook and the React notes are paid for in every session, although they matter in only a few.
  • The greeting carries no information.
9dd8ed3017: The fixed version is shorter than the broken one's runbook alone. The secret moved to a secret store, backed by a Read(./.env) deny rule. The guard rails are enforced in settings and only mentioned here. The runbook became a Skill. The React notes became a path-scoped rule for **/*.tsx. One build tool remains. An import pulls in the ADR index rather than copying it.
f9fac4f66c:
Scope answers "who should this line affect?" The rule of thumb mirrors the settings files:

  • What the team needs goes in the committed project file.
  • What only you want goes in your user file (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) or in a personal project file that is not committed.
  • What the organisation requires goes in the managed CLAUDE.md that IT deploys.

The classic incident is a senior developer's conventions living in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Their sessions follow the convention. New joiners' sessions don't. The team concludes the model is inconsistent. The fix is to move the lines to the project file, and to verify on a fresh clone with /memory.

The reverse fault is just as real. Commit personal preferences ("answer tersely", "I use fish shell") to the project file, and you impose one person's taste on forty sessions.
25991d5405: Review answers "who may change it, and how do we know a change is good?" Treat a CLAUDE.md change like a change to a shared build script:
19165df008: Ownership. Put CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/ and .claude/settings.json under CODEOWNERS, so a platform or tech-lead group reviews them. A one-line edit there affects every session in the repo.
53a5ee9c8a: Lint in CI. A cheap script catches most faults. It checks the size budget (lines or estimated tokens) and secret patterns. It flags enforcement words ("never", "must not") that have no matching deny rule or hook, imports that point at missing files, and conflicting commands. 04_claude_md_lint.py implements these checks.
bb39097451: Behavioural check for significant changes. Run a handful of representative tasks headless (claude -p) before and after the change, and compare outcomes. Did the build command change? Did a convention start or stop being applied? This is a small eval, not a unit test.
3bb8e7dcb9: Staleness. Commands and paths in CLAUDE.md rot when the build changes. A CI step that runs each command listed under "Build and test" catches the rot on the day it happens.
5b407251cd:
Learn to read the stems:

  • "New team members' sessions do not follow a convention that seniors' sessions follow" points to user-level placement.
  • "A rule in CLAUDE.md is usually followed but was violated once in production" points to enforcement in settings or a hook, not to stronger wording.
  • "The CLAUDE.md is 800 lines and the model ignores parts of it" points to splitting into rules and Skills, not to adding emphasis.
6c94645232: CLAUDE.md is read by the model. settings.json is read by Claude Code. Its keys select the model, permission rules and the default permission mode, hooks, environment variables for the session, enabled plugins and known marketplaces, credential helpers such as apiKeyHelper, and many interface options. The documentation describes four files plus delivery mechanisms for managed policy:
b0a099f10d: A fifth file, ~/.claude.json, is written by Claude Code itself. It holds sign-in state, user-scope MCP server configurations, per-project trust decisions and the global config keys that /config writes. You don't normally edit it, and it is not part of the settings precedence stack.
8c6cd880b3: Scalars: highest level wins. Say the team file sets "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5" and your local file sets "model": "claude-opus-5-5". Only your sessions use Opus, because project local sits above shared project. If managed settings set a key, nothing below can change it, including --settings.
a8488c3e83: Lists merge. permissions.allow entries from user, project and local files are combined; no file replaces another. Each file can add entries without deleting another file's. The documentation notes that a few model-list keys follow their own rules (check the docs for those keys).
f9c0b8bf94: Environment variables are not a level. Each variable that pairs with a key has its own rule. ANTHROPIC_MODEL exported in your shell overrides the model key from any file. ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL applies only when no file sets model.
1fe65149eb: A few restrictive keys invert precedence. For some security keys, a stricter value from a lower scope is honoured even when managed settings are looser. Examples are permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories: true from any scope, or a lower maxEffortLevel cap. The idea is simple: anyone may make their own session safer, and nobody below managed may make it less safe.
8c013bd77c:
Two more behaviours explain "I committed it but it doesn't apply to my teammates".

First, some keys are ignored in a repository file. The settings reference marks each key's scope. Keys scoped to "user, local or managed" or "managed" never take effect from .claude/settings.json. A cloned repository should not be able to grant itself, say, a credential helper.

Second, permissions.allow rules and additionalDirectories in a project file grant capability. Claude Code applies them only after the user accepts the workspace trust dialog for that folder. Deny and ask rules apply immediately, since they only restrict.

Headless claude -p runs and SDK sessions never show the trust dialog, and that matters in CI (check the docs for which repository content applies there).
f7e7b03ecc:
Settings files are strict JSON. Comments and trailing commas are errors, reported at startup. A $schema line pointing at the published schema (https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json) gives you editor validation, though the schema can lag the newest releases.

Claude Code watches the files and applies most edits, including permissions and hooks, without a restart. A few keys are read only at session start. /status lists which sources loaded, but it doesn't say which file supplied each key. claude doctor lists rejected entries.
9543e0493f:
Each block comes with an owner question:

  • model: should the team share a default, or should each developer choose?
  • permissions: what is safe for everyone without asking, what needs a human, and what is never allowed?
  • env: which variables does the session need? Never secrets; use a credential helper or the developer's environment.
  • hooks: which deterministic checks are too contextual for a pattern?
  • enabledPlugins and extraKnownMarketplaces: what is the team's toolset? Review it like dependencies.

01_settings_merge.py reproduces the merge rules over four layers.
79dfa769f6:
Precedence rules are easy to recite and easy to misapply. A real session loads five or six sources at once, and different keys follow different rules. The way to make the rules stick is to resolve one realistic stack by hand, key by key, the way Claude Code does at startup.

The stack below belongs to a developer, Asha, on the order-platform team. Her organisation deploys managed settings. The repository has a committed team file. She has a personal user file and a local override. Today she launched with a one-off --settings file for a spike.
d2911f23c6: Resolve it in the order Claude Code applies the rules. First decide which entries are even eligible. Then merge lists, then pick scalars, then resolve maps per entry.
044a160cd0: Eligibility. The team file sets apiKeyHelper. A credential helper is the kind of key the settings reference scopes to user, local or managed files, because a cloned repository must not choose the program that produces your credentials. From .claude/settings.json it is ignored (check the per-key scope column in the docs for the exact list). The second eligibility question is whether Asha has accepted the workspace trust dialog for this folder. Suppose this is a fresh clone and she has not. The project file's allow entries grant capability, so they wait for trust. Its ask and deny entries only restrict, so they apply immediately.
325e71f7cb: Lists merge. With trust not yet accepted, the effective allow is Bash(*) (user). ask is Bash(git push *) (project). deny is the union of Bash(kubectl * --context=prod*) (managed), WebFetch (command line) and Read(./.env) (project). Nothing was replaced. Each file contributed.
88fdf8fc40: Scalars. model is set by user (Opus), project (Sonnet) and local (Opus). The highest level that sets it wins, which is local, so Opus. Managed doesn't set model. It sets availableModels, which restricts what may be chosen, and Opus is on the list, so the choice stands. disableBypassPermissionsMode comes only from managed, and nothing below could have changed it anyway.
a286b0bd83: Maps per entry. env resolves variable by variable. SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE is local, because local beats project. ORDER_TOPIC_PREFIX is order., since only the project sets it. JAVA_HOME comes from user. Three files contribute to one map.
839a56b411: Outside the stack. If Asha's shell exports ANTHROPIC_MODEL, that variable outranks every file's model key. /model during the session outranks the variable (see the model trace later in this chapter). Environment variables are not one more file in the stack. Each has its own documented relationship to its key.
a1749b4de4:
Two conclusions from the trace deserve a plain statement, because exam distractors contradict them.

First, file precedence and permission evaluation are different mechanisms. Precedence chooses a scalar such as model. Permissions are not chosen. They are pooled, and then the pooled rules are evaluated deny, ask, allow. So "the project file is lower than local, therefore a local allow overrides a project deny" is wrong in a way that sounds right.

Second, "I committed it" is not "it applies". A committed key may be ineligible from a repo file. A committed allow may be waiting on a trust decision that a new joiner hasn't made yet. When a teammate says the team settings do nothing for them, ask two questions first: which keys, and did they trust the folder?
13f6732ada:
Spring Boot resolves a property by walking an ordered list of property sources (command-line arguments, environment, profile-specific files, application.yml, defaults). It takes the first source that defines the key. That is exactly how Claude Code picks a scalar.

Lists are where the two differ. In Spring Boot, when more than one source defines a list property, the higher source replaces the whole list. There is no element-wise merge. A Spring engineer who carries that intuition over will expect a local permissions.allow to replace the team's allow list, or a personal file to replace a team deny list. Neither happens.

The design reason is security. If a higher-precedence personal file could replace a permission list, any developer could silently delete the team's denies. Merging, plus deny-first evaluation, means anyone can add restrictions and nobody below managed can remove them.
907072f74e:
The trailing comma and comments make the whole file invalid JSON. None of it applies, and startup reports an error that people dismiss.

Fix the syntax and the deny applies at once. The credential helper is still ignored, though, and the allow still waits for trust. Don't fight those two rules. Move the credential helper to managed settings or to each developer's user file. Add the trust step to the onboarding checklist ("open the repo, accept trust, run /status and check the project source is listed").
75145e08ea: 17_settings_trace.py resolves this stack with provenance for every key. It models the trust gate and the repo-ineligible keys, and prints the table above. Treat its list of repo-ineligible keys as data to refresh from the settings reference.
ed80db08ff:
Permission rules are the main enforcement surface in settings. The exam tests their evaluation order more than their syntax. The documented order is simple: deny, then ask, then allow; the first match in that order decides, and specificity does not change the order.

So a broad Bash(aws *) in deny blocks aws s3 ls, even if an allow rule names it exactly. An allow rule can't carve an exception out of a deny. A matching ask rule prompts even when a narrower allow also matches. A call that matches nothing falls through to the permission mode's default behaviour, which in the default mode means prompting.
babf648dec:
Three pitfalls are worth memorising. Each produces rules that look right and do nothing.

The single-slash path. Read(/secrets/**) written in user settings blocks ~/.claude/secrets/**, not a secrets folder in your project. A single leading slash anchors at the settings source. Use // for absolute paths, or a relative pattern for project paths (03_path_anchor.py).

Rules for the wrong tool. File permission checks consult only Read(...) and Edit(...) rules. A Write(docs/**) rule is accepted and never consulted, with a startup warning. A Read deny also blocks Edit and Write on the same path.

Bash patterns are not a sandbox. A Bash rule matches the command text Claude writes, after splitting compound commands and stripping known wrappers. It doesn't match the same program invoked by absolute path or inside sh -c. Deny and ask rules do apply to every subcommand of a compound command, and inside substitutions. For a hard network or filesystem boundary, pair rules with the sandbox or an OS-level control. This is the same lesson as chapter 19: a pattern on text is a guard rail, not an isolation boundary.
7c3e3b5be9: Bash(*) allows every command. The deny covers only one literal string, so rm -rf ./ runs. Read(/secrets/**) in a project file anchors at the settings source. That happens to work for a project file, but the same line copied to user settings protects nothing in the repo. Write(...) is never consulted.
b2434b75de:
Permission modes (defaultMode) set the baseline for calls that no rule matches. Documented values include default, acceptEdits, plan, auto and bypassPermissions (check the docs for the full current list).

Setting permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode and permissions.disableAutoMode to "disable" prevents those modes. They are most useful in managed settings, where developers can't remove them. Managed settings can also restrict which rules count at all, for example through a managed-only permission rules key (check the docs for the exact name).

02_permission_eval.py implements the evaluation order and the wildcard rules, and asserts the cases above.
6e3aee4326: Evaluation rules only become exam answers when you can apply them to a specific call. This section runs seven calls against one merged rule set. Then it looks at the two places where evaluation surprises people: commands that contain other commands, and calls that match no rule at all.
92a380e411:
Row four is the one to understand. Claude Code splits a compound command at operators such as &&, ; and pipes. Deny and ask rules apply to every part, including command substitutions. That closes the obvious bypass of hiding a denied command behind an allowed one.

For an allow to let the whole command through silently, every part needs to be covered. When one part isn't, you are prompted (check the docs for the exact rule on allow matching across compound commands, and for the list of wrappers stripped before matching).

The wrong mental model is "the rule matches the start of the string". Under it, git diff && rm -rf build would run unprompted, because it starts with an allowed prefix.
c011f73fb5:
Most calls in a real session match no rule. What happens then is the permission mode's decision. That's why defaultMode is part of the security configuration and not a convenience.

  • In default mode, an unmatched call prompts. Reads are generally permitted without prompting (check the docs for the per-tool defaults).
  • acceptEdits auto-approves file edits in the working directory.
  • plan keeps Claude to read-only exploration.
  • auto lets a classifier approve or block calls that no rule decides. You can turn it off with disableAutoMode.
  • bypassPermissions runs unmatched calls without asking. Deny rules still apply there. That's why the deny list must be right before anyone uses bypass mode in a container.

The configuration lesson: rules handle the cases you anticipated, and the mode handles everything else. A team should choose both deliberately.
8691e669b0:
A headless run has nobody to prompt. Every call the job needs must be decided by a rule or by the mode. Pattern rules match the command text Claude writes, and Claude doesn't always write the command the way the pattern author did. The fix is a deliberately chosen pattern for the run, plus a deny list for what must never happen.

Flags such as --allowedTools add per-run rules; check the docs for how they combine with settings files in your version. 18_compound_bash.py implements subcommand splitting with deny, ask and allow, and asserts every row of the trace table.
1f4477fb7d:
The env block sets environment variables for the Claude Code session and the processes it starts. Use it for non-secret configuration the project needs (SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE, a test database URL for local containers). Use it also for Claude Code's own variables, for example to remap a model alias.

Secrets don't belong in a committed env block. Claude Code supports credential helpers (apiKeyHelper) and the developer's own environment for that. Some variables are ignored when they come from a repository file, notably telemetry export settings. The reason is the same as for keys: a cloned repo should not redirect your data.
e1214e8178:
The hooks block maps lifecycle events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart, ConfigChange and others) to matchers and handlers. From a configuration-management view, the questions are where the hook is declared and who can remove it.

  • A hook in the committed project file is reviewed with the code and runs for the whole team.
  • A hook in managed settings runs for everyone and can't be removed below managed.
  • A plugin can ship hooks too, which is one reason plugin installation is a dependency decision.

Hook scripts live in the repo (referenced through $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR) or in the plugin (through ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}). Either way, they are versioned with what they protect. Exit code 2 from a PreToolUse command blocks the call and returns stderr to Claude; chapter 20 covers the protocol. The ConfigChange event fires when Claude Code detects a settings-file change, which is useful for auditing configuration edits made mid-session.
3cb1e3a302:
Model keys. model sets the session's starting model. Model precedence differs from ordinary keys, because flags and variables take part. The documented order, highest first, is:

  1. /model chosen during the session;
  2. --model;
  3. ANTHROPIC_MODEL;
  4. the model setting;
  5. ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL.

Project and managed model settings reapply at each launch, overriding a choice saved earlier with /model. Organisations restrict choices with availableModels in managed settings. Its entries match a family alias, a version prefix or a full ID. Organisations can also declare fallbackModel entries, tried when the primary is overloaded or unavailable. Section 11 explains why a Claude Code alias like sonnet is a floating reference, and how to pin it.
3b95bddfb7: 05_config_placement.py sorts requirements into these destinations from a few features: must it always hold, who does it affect, and is it personal? It makes a quick self-test.
f4ee1c91af: Pinning only makes sense once you know what each identifier promises. Anthropic's documentation (the model IDs and versions page) says it directly: "Each Claude model ID identifies a pinned version of the model ... the underlying model remains constant for the lifetime of that ID". It adds: "Anthropic does not update the weights or configuration of an existing model ID. When an updated version is available, it ships under a new model ID." In practice there are three kinds of identifier:
ed4e86a401:
The exam-relevant consequences follow. In an API application on a current model, writing claude-sonnet-5-5 is already a pin. The ID will not start serving different weights. What changes the model under you is one of these:

  • (a) a pre-4.6 alias;
  • (b) a Claude Code alias such as sonnet, which resolved to a different model per provider even on the day this was written (the docs list Sonnet 5.5 on the Anthropic API, and older Sonnet versions on some cloud providers);
  • (c) a gateway or platform that maps a logical name to an ID;
  • (d) your own configuration, if it reads a model name from a place someone else edits.

The documentation adds a nuance worth knowing. Weights are fixed per ID, but the serving infrastructure (routing, safety classifiers, sampling implementation) can change. So small observable differences on a stable ID are possible. Pinning removes the large source of drift, not every source. Monitoring still matters.
0e37ece3fc:
Platform formats differ, and you must take them from the platform. Bedrock dateless IDs look like anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 (older ones look like anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0), and Claude Code on Bedrock pins with an inference profile ARN. Google Cloud uses the Claude API format from 4.6 on, and claude-haiku-4-5@20251001 for older models.

A config value valid on one provider is invalid on another. That's a reason to keep the provider and the model ID together in one typed configuration object.
f0348af1e2:
Claude Code accepts a full model ID anywhere it accepts an alias. So the simplest pin is "model": "claude-opus-5-5" in project or managed settings.

You can also keep the convenient alias names while fixing what they mean. The documented environment variables ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL remap the aliases. CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL sets the subagent default. An organisation that must keep everyone on approved versions combines availableModels with a pinned model in managed settings.
dd07e93e8e: Model selection in Claude Code is the setting people misread most. Five mechanisms can name a model, and each can carry two kinds of name (alias and full ID). Resolve it the way you resolved the settings stack. Walk the precedence ladder from the top, stop at the first source that names a model, then resolve the name.
1b24559c99:
Case 1, the team default. The committed file has "model": "sonnet", and nobody sets a flag or variable. The source is the setting. The name is an alias, and no remap is set. So the session uses whatever Sonnet this Claude Code version maps sonnet to on this provider.

Today, on the Anthropic API, that is Sonnet 5.5. After a Claude Code update it may be a newer Sonnet. On a cloud provider it may be an older one. The team believes it pinned a model. It has pinned a family.
ab0181b1c7:
Case 2, the CI override. The CI image exports ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5 for a review job, and the committed file says claude-sonnet-5-5. The variable outranks the setting, so the job uses Opus.

Later, someone wonders why the review job costs more than developer sessions running the "same configuration". It isn't the same configuration. One input lives in the CI image, outside the repository's settings files. This is exactly the drift the per-session tuple log exists to expose.
988113a11a:
Case 3, the restricted organisation. Managed settings pin "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", with availableModels listing Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5. A developer picks Opus with /model for a hard refactor. That's allowed, since it's on the list, and it lasts for the session. At the next launch the managed model reapplies. If the developer tries Haiku, the restriction refuses it.

What happens when an environment variable names a model outside availableModels? Check that detail in the docs before relying on it in an exam answer.
493b0f71af:
The fixed form keeps aliases usable for humans (typing /model opus still works) while making them mean a fixed ID. It also moves the per-job override out of an invisible environment and into the reviewed workflow file.

The JSON output of a headless run includes per-model usage. That's the cheapest place to record the served model (check the docs for the exact field layout in your version). 19_model_precedence.py resolves the ladder for all three cases.
e0308d4ab0: The model lineup at the time of writing (verified 2026-10-09) is below. Use it to recognise current IDs in exam options. When you build, take exact IDs and prices from the models overview page, because they change faster than any study guide.
794a302cfc: Consider a service that pinned claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 for triage a year ago. It is correctly pinned and still works. It is also running an older generation than Haiku 5.5. Pinning protects you from surprise changes. It doesn't tell you when to move. That is the job of the lifecycle process in the next section.
49d75eac4d:
A pin is not permanent, because the pinned model has a lifecycle. The deprecations page defines four stages:

  • Active: fully supported and recommended.
  • Legacy: no further updates; may be deprecated.
  • Deprecated: still works, not recommended; a replacement and a retirement date are assigned.
  • Retired: "Requests to retired models will fail".

Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice before retiring a publicly released model. Bedrock and Google Cloud set their own schedules. Recent entries show the cadence. claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 was deprecated 2026-09-30, with retirement on 2026-11-30 and claude-sonnet-5-5 as the replacement. claude-3-haiku-20240307 retired 2026-04-20.
b496d33d77:
If nobody is watching, retirement turns a quality decision into an availability incident. The controls are mechanical:

  • a registry of every model ID in use, by service and role;
  • a scheduled check of each ID against the lifecycle data;
  • an alert at deprecation, with the retirement date as a due date.

The deprecations page recommends exporting usage from the Console Usage page to find remaining calls by API key and model. That catches the service nobody remembered. 07_deprecation_check.py runs the check over a sample registry.
397c195dfc: The new model may need a new prompt version. Models differ in verbosity, instruction following and formatting habits. So the candidate is really "model B with prompt vN" or "model B with prompt vN+1". That's why section 14 versions the prompt and model together. Breaking changes to check on every upgrade:
54e6ada1d8:
The older heuristic "a pinned ID ends in eight digits" is now wrong. It rejects claude-sonnet-5-5, which is a fixed snapshot. Teams that kept it either disabled the check or pinned to deprecated models.

The guard above classifies the three kinds explicitly. Keep the alias lists as data, and review them when Anthropic publishes new models (06_model_id_classify.py). The Spring form follows.
657e4c4b1f:
The upgrade pipeline above describes what happens to one candidate. A migration forced by a deprecation notice is a different problem, because the date isn't yours. The notice gives a retirement date, and after it, "Requests to retired models will fail".

Some steps take calendar time: finding callers, building or refreshing an eval set, adapting a prompt, letting a canary run long enough to see weekly traffic patterns. You have to schedule every one of them backwards from that date. The schedule has to exist before the notice, as a template, so the notice only fills in a date.

Teams that treat the notice as the start of design work routinely discover they need four weeks for an eval set they don't have, inside an eight-week window.
936e9d03a5:
Inventory is the step most often underestimated. The registry of model IDs (from the section on lifecycle) lists what the platform team knows about. It misses the notebook a data team runs nightly, the CI job that summarises pull requests, and the vendor integration configured in a console.

Two sources close the gap. Usage exports from the Console, broken down by model and API key, show traffic the registry doesn't explain. A repository-wide search for model ID patterns (including environment files and infrastructure templates) shows callers that aren't sending traffic yet.

Each caller gets an owner and a role (triage, agent, planner). The replacement is chosen per role, not per ID. A deprecated Sonnet used for bulk classification might move to claude-haiku-5-5 ($0.10 / $0.50 per million input / output tokens) instead of the like-for-like successor, if the evals say quality holds.
fc1acfb63d:
Offline evaluation runs the incumbent's eval set, unchanged, on both models and reports per slice. You usually need two candidates: the replacement with the current prompt bundle, and the replacement with an adapted bundle. Running both separates "the model is worse at this" from "the prompt was tuned to the old model's habits".

The chapter 05 parameter changes matter here as integration failures, not quality ones. The newer models can reject outright a request that sets non-default sampling parameters, forces tool_choice, or uses assistant prefill. So the first eval run is effectively an integration test. Those failures are cheap to find offline and expensive to find in a canary.
25ba1af73d:
Shadow traffic sits between offline evals and a canary. The incumbent still serves every request. The candidate is called on a copy of a sample of live requests, and its output is logged and compared, never returned.

It answers a question an offline set can't: does this month's live input distribution contain cases the eval set lacks? The comparison metric is agreement on the decision the application acts on (the routed queue, the extracted fields). Textual similarity is the wrong metric, because two correct answers rarely share wording.

Shadowing costs a second model call per sampled request, and it must not double side effects. A shadow call allowed to execute tools would send the email twice. So shadow requests run with tools stubbed, or with read-only tools only.
0f6a8cc3da:
The fixed form keeps both IDs in configuration for the whole window. That's what makes rollback a one-line change. It also lets each role move at its own pace. Here, triage is in canary on a cheaper model with a new prompt version, while the agent role is still only shadowing a like-for-like replacement.

The deprecated ID leaves configuration as the last step, after promotion has held. A CI check (the lifecycle check from earlier) then fails any pull request that brings it back.
db26ed5e01:
Two operational details decide whether the shadow is safe. The shadow executor is bounded and drops work when full, so a slow candidate can't exhaust threads on the serving path. And shadow calls carry their own rate-limit budget. Doubling traffic on one API key can push the incumbent into 429s and turn a measurement into an outage.

Expect cost to change during the window for a second reason. Prompt-cache entries are tied to the exact request prefix and model, so the first calls to the new model start with a cold cache (for how caches behave across models, check the docs).

Platform schedules differ too. Bedrock and Google Cloud publish their own deprecation dates, so a service running the same model on two providers has two deadlines.
5b4ab4f814:
A prompt is source code written in natural language. It needs the controls source code has: history, review, tests, controlled rollout, rollback.

The unit to version is not the system prompt string alone. It is the prompt bundle: system prompt, user template, few-shot examples, tool schema versions, output schema, model ID and generation settings. They change meaning together. A system prompt tuned for one model's verbosity is a different artefact on another model. A tool description edit changes which tool gets chosen, just as surely as a prompt edit. So changing only the model under an unchanged prompt still makes a new bundle version.
5f84a00fb2:
Each design point in that code is tied to a failure:

  • The hash covers the canonical JSON, so a whitespace-only edit that slipped into a published version is detectable.
  • The pointer file is separate from the bundles. Promotion and rollback are one-line config changes that can be reviewed and audited without touching prompt text.
  • model_served comes from the response, not the config.
  • Template substitution uses a plain replace on a known placeholder rather than str.format, which would break on braces inside customer text.
  • If you use prompt caching, keep the stable bundle content at the front of the request. Editing early text invalidates the cached prefix, and that shows up as a cost jump on the version that changed it (chapter 15).
5987d85e2d: The registry service is where unreviewed changes creep back in. A UI that lets someone edit the active prompt in place recreates the spreadsheet era. Whatever the store, require immutable versions, a review step before a version becomes active, and an audit log of pointer moves. 09_prompt_bundle_hash.py and 10_prompt_registry.py implement both halves.
60417d8c07:
Immutable integers are enough to roll back. They aren't enough to communicate risk: "v7 to v8" says nothing about whether downstream parsers will break.

Teams that run many prompts add meaning to version numbers. They borrow semantic versioning and define what counts as a breaking change for a prompt. The definitions below are a convention, not an Anthropic feature. That's the point: you write them down so reviewers apply the same test.
24945bb96a:
The last row matters more than it looks. With code, a typo fix in a comment is provably neutral. With prompts, no edit is provably neutral. The model reads the whole text, and rewording can move a borderline slice.

Patch means "we expect no change", and the eval is how you check that expectation. A rule that skips evals for patches just recreates the in-place edit problem with extra steps.
e0883b97b2:
Because the bundle pins a model, a model upgrade produces a new bundle. A team running several bundles across several models needs to know which pairs have been evaluated. A compatibility matrix makes that visible. Rows are bundle versions, columns are model IDs, and cells hold the eval result. Only evaluated pairs may be deployed.

The matrix also explains a common surprise during a model upgrade. The best prompt for the new model is often not the incumbent prompt. So the comparison that matters is "best known bundle on A" against "best known bundle on B", not "same prompt, two models".
8484d7816b:
Prompts are templates, and template engines have opinions about braces, escapes and missing variables. Customer text and code snippets contain braces. So does a JSON example inside a system prompt.

Python's str.format treats every brace as a placeholder. A bundle that worked in review fails in production the first time a ticket contains {. Worse, a JSON example in the template can silently lose its braces. The fix is a substitution that only touches declared placeholders and fails loudly on undeclared ones.
442e9f0e59:
The declared-slot set belongs in the bundle. Then the CI check can verify that a template change didn't add or drop a slot without the code changing too. Under the convention above, that is a major-version change.

The single-pass substitution inserts a value containing {{x}} literally, without expanding it. 20_prompt_semver.py classifies a diff between two bundles as major, minor or patch, and includes this renderer with its failure cases.
3c8d40242f:
For this reader, the production registry is likely a Spring service. The structure maps one to one:

  • an immutable record per bundle version;
  • a loader that hashes canonical content;
  • per-profile pointer configuration;
  • the tuple written to the MDC, so every log line in the request carries it.
59b5c797bc:
Watch for two Spring-specific traps. First, don't load bundles with @Value placeholders. Spring's own ${...} resolution will try to expand any dollar-brace sequence inside prompt text. Second, don't make the pointer map refreshable through an unauthenticated actuator endpoint. That's the registry UI problem again, with a different front end.

Promotion is a reviewed change to the pointer configuration. Or it's an audited call to a release service that checks the eval result for that exact bundle and model pair before it moves the pointer.
dcc04dd6fd:
You can't judge a prompt or model change by inspection, and an aggregate score hides the failures that generate complaints. So the gate has three properties:

  • It runs the same versioned dataset for incumbent and candidate, so differences come from the change.
  • It checks per-slice thresholds (per category, per language, per customer tier), not only the mean. A change that improves billing by four points and drops porting by six does not ship.
  • It compares cost and latency. A prompt that adds 2,000 tokens of examples may be better and still unaffordable.

Chapter 04 covers eval design. The point here is that the gate is wired into the change path: a CI check on every pull request touching prompts/, model configuration or tool schemas.
dab226fad3:
Canary assignment should be deterministic per user or conversation: hash the ID into buckets. Then a customer doesn't flip between versions mid-conversation, and you can match a complaint to the version that served it.

Rollback should be automatic for hard signals (structured-output parse failure rate, tool error rate) and human-decided for soft ones. Keep the previous model ID and prompt version deployable until the new one has run at full traffic for an agreed period. For a model upgrade, keep it until the old model's retirement makes that moot. 12_canary_rollout.py simulates bucketing, a regression in one slice, and automatic rollback.
2b5ef4ed78:
Java teams will recognise the pattern from feature-flag platforms. The prompt version and model ID are flag values. The flag is evaluated per request with a stable key. The flag platform's audit log is the change history.

What differs is the test. Unit tests check a flag guarding code before rollout. An eval dataset checks a flag guarding a prompt before rollout, and online metrics check it during rollout.
db2c3c919d:
The pieces (immutable versions, pointers, the gate, canary, automatic rollback) are easiest to remember as one release followed end to end, including the part where it goes wrong.

The service is ticket routing for a telecom support desk, and production points at triage@6. A developer wants billing disputes that mention a charge to go to the billing queue rather than general. 23_rollback_trace.py replays this trace.
41ac40a72c:
Three decisions in that trace are exam material.

First, the gate passed and the release was still wrong. Offline evals bound the risk to the cases you have, which is why canary and a cheap rollback exist. The right response isn't to make the gate infinitely strict. It's to add the missing cases after each incident, so the dataset builds up the organisation's failure history.

Second, rollback didn't need a build. If rollback is git revert plus a deploy pipeline, the time to recover is the pipeline's duration, and teams under pressure skip steps. A pointer move gets reviewed after the fact, through the audit log.

Third, the fix didn't edit v7. Editing it would have made the per-call log lie: conversations logged as v7 on day 4 would point at text that didn't serve them.
5f1819204e:
What the trace doesn't show is just as useful. Rollback was safe because v7 hadn't changed the output contract: v6 and v7 both emit {"queue": ...}.

Suppose v7 had been a major version, with a new field consumed downstream. Rolling the prompt back would break the consumer that had started reading the new field. So major versions first roll out behind a consumer that accepts both shapes. It's the same expand-and-contract discipline used for database schema changes.

And rollback doesn't fix the conversations already misrouted. The per-call log is what lets operations find and re-route them.
ce133a7ec7:
Spring teams have a ready analogue. A Git-backed Config Server serves properties per application and profile. Clients re-read them with @RefreshScope and /actuator/refresh (or a bus event). Git history is the audit log.

Mapping the registry onto it works for pointers. llm.triage.prompt-version=7 in triage-prod.yml is a pointer, and changing it in Git and refreshing is a pointer move.

It breaks in two places. A refresh changes the value for every subsequent request at once. Without a sticky per-conversation key, a customer can flip versions mid-conversation, so the service must compute the canary bucket from the conversation ID, not from the refreshed property alone. And Config Server is a poor home for the bundles themselves. Prompt text contains ${...} and braces that property resolution tries to expand, and properties have no content hash.

Keep bundles as immutable files or registry records. Let the config server carry only pointers and percentages.
1ae8715e33:
Every section so far ends in a check: lint CLAUDE.md, validate settings JSON, refuse moving model IDs, hash and gate prompt bundles, validate plugins. Those checks only protect you if they run on the changes that need them.

The practical design is a router in CI that maps changed paths to required checks. A pull request that touches prompts/ can't merge without the eval gate. One that touches .claude/settings.json can't merge without a settings validation and a code-owner review. It's the same idea as path-filtered workflows in any monorepo, applied to inputs the compiler ignores.
328a2f5db1:
Two design choices make the router useful rather than decorative.

It fails closed. A changed file under a configuration directory that matches no rule fails the build. So a new kind of configuration file (a new rules folder, a second MCP config) forces a decision about how it gets checked.

And the checks are owned. With CODEOWNERS on each path, the eval gate isn't only run; someone accountable for that feature reads its result. 21_config_ci_router.py implements the mapping and the fail-closed rule.
9e11d4c05d:
CI checks what is in the repository. Much of the effective configuration isn't there: user settings, local overrides, exported environment variables, managed settings that differ between a contractor laptop and an employee laptop, plugins installed at user scope.

When two developers get different behaviour from "the same repo", the fastest diagnosis is to compare effective configuration, not files. Interactively, run /status on each machine to see the loaded sources. In automation, write the effective model, permission lists, enabled plugins with versions, and the relevant environment variables to the run log, then diff two runs. The diff below is typical.
02f1d78b76: The diff points straight at the causes: a personal model override, a personal allow-everything rule, a local profile, and a plugin that auto-updated on one machine. None of these is wrong for a personal session. All of them are wrong to assume away when comparing results. 22_config_drift.py computes the diff with provenance.
53d3f66a17:
Chapter 09 covered what a plugin bundles and how marketplaces and install scopes work. The configuration-management question is narrower: what does a plugin depend on, how do those dependencies resolve, and how do you keep the result reproducible?

A plugin has three kinds of dependency:

  • other plugins, whose skills or MCP tools it calls;
  • packages and binaries its hooks and servers run (an npm MCP server, jq, a JVM);
  • configuration it needs from the user (endpoints, tokens).

Each needs a declared version or a check.
fc2bedb2aa:
The manifest field is dependencies in .claude-plugin/plugin.json. Each entry takes one of three forms:

  • a plugin name, resolved in the declaring plugin's own marketplace;
  • "name@marketplace";
  • an object with name, an optional marketplace, and an optional version holding a semantic-version range in npm syntax (~2.1.0, ^2.0, >=1.4, =2.1.0).

Without a range, the dependency tracks whatever version its marketplace publishes on the next update. If that release renames an MCP tool your plugin calls, your plugin breaks for everyone who updates.
f2a6a49377:
Resolution works against git tags. For git-backed sources, the dependency installs at the highest tag that satisfies the range. Tags must be named <plugin-name>--v<version> (for example secrets-vault--v2.1.0), so one marketplace repository can host several plugins with independent histories.

claude plugin tag --push creates the tag. Before it does, it validates the plugin, checks that plugin.json and the marketplace entry agree on the version, and requires a clean tree. Ranges don't match pre-releases unless the range opts in (^2.0.0-0).

For npm, archive or command sources, the range doesn't choose what is fetched. It is checked at load, and the dependent plugin is disabled if the installed version doesn't satisfy it.
d9cf207771:
When several installed plugins constrain the same dependency, it resolves to the highest version that satisfies all ranges.

  • Non-overlapping ranges make the second install fail with a "conflicting version requirements" message.
  • An exact pin (=2.1.0) holds the dependency there. Auto-update skips newer versions while the pinning plugin is installed.
  • Auto-update of a constrained dependency moves only within the intersection of installed ranges.
  • When the last constraining plugin is uninstalled, the dependency goes back to tracking its marketplace.

claude plugin list shows a tag-resolved dependency with a commit suffix such as 2.1.0-8713c5b11005. claude plugin prune removes auto-installed dependencies that nothing needs. 13_plugin_dep_resolve.py implements this resolution over a tag list, including the conflict case.
b8b9517b30:
Cross-marketplace dependencies are refused by default. Say a plugin from marketplace A depends on a plugin in marketplace B. It is not installed unless A's marketplace.json lists B in allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn, or the user already has the dependency enabled at the same scope.

This stops one marketplace from silently installing code from a source the user never reviewed. It's the plugin equivalent of a dependency-confusion attack. Only the root marketplace's allowlist counts (14_cross_marketplace.py).
f8a41d150d: The plugin's own version in plugin.json pins users to that version until you change it, and the manifest value overrides the marketplace entry's. Bump it on every behavioural change, and tag the release. Otherwise dependants' ranges can't resolve to it.
deb0c16995: Package versions inside the plugin. An MCP server started with npx -y @acme/orders-mcp fetches the latest package at each start, which defeats every other pin. Use an exact version (@acme/orders-mcp@2.3.1), or vendor the server.
103684c91d: Paths. Reference bundled files with ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}. It changes on each update, so never write state there. Put installed dependencies, caches and generated files under ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}, which persists across updates under ~/.claude/plugins/data/<id>/.
38db0e87c6: User configuration and secrets. Declare required values in userConfig. Options marked sensitive go to the platform credential store, not to settings.json. Reference them as ${user_config.KEY} in MCP and LSP config, or read CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY> in hooks.
9df7e48608:
A platform team can publish a bundle plugin whose manifest contains only a name, a version and a dependencies list. Installing it installs the whole set. Adding a plugin to the standard set means a new bundle version, reviewed and tagged like any release.

Teams enable the bundle in the committed .claude/settings.json (enabledPlugins, with the marketplace in extraKnownMarketplaces). Organisations that require it put it in managed enabledPlugins. They can also restrict which marketplaces may be added at all, through managed settings (a strict known-marketplaces key; check the docs for the exact name and shape).

The result has the same structure as an internal Maven repository with a parent POM: one curated source, version ranges reviewed by a platform team, and a managed baseline developers can't remove.
4b0b8455e9:
The resolution rules for plugin dependencies are short. The cases that break are graphs. Walk one install sequence on a developer machine, with these tags published in the marketplace repository:

  • secrets-vault--v2.0.3, --v2.1.0, --v2.1.4, --v2.2.0, --v3.0.0-rc.1, --v3.0.1;
  • audit-logger--v1.2.0, --v1.3.0.
10b1a1e32e: Install deploy-kit 3.1.0, which depends on secrets-vault ~2.1.0 and on audit-logger with no range. The candidates for ~2.1.0 are 2.1.0 and 2.1.4. The highest is chosen: secrets-vault 2.1.4. audit-logger has no range, so it installs the marketplace's current version, 1.3.0, and will track the marketplace on later updates.
9d1e66d9e5: Install release-bot 1.4.0, which depends on secrets-vault ^2.0. The installed constraints are now ~2.1.0 and ^2.0. Their intersection is 2.1.x, and the highest satisfying tag is still 2.1.4. Nothing changes on disk. Note that ^2.0 alone would have chosen 2.2.0. The stricter co-installed range wins, because both must hold.
21cdd38ae2: Auto-update runs after secrets-vault--v2.1.5 is tagged. That tag is inside the intersection, so the dependency moves to 2.1.5. Then --v2.2.1 is tagged. It is outside ~2.1.0, so the dependency stays put. The release candidate 3.0.0-rc.1 is never considered, since ranges don't match pre-releases unless they opt in.
0947a50fc5: Install legacy-ops 0.9.0, which requires ~3.0. The intersection of ~2.1.0, ^2.0 and ~3.0 is empty. The install fails with a conflicting-version message, and the existing plugins are untouched. The fix belongs to a plugin author, not to the installer. Either legacy-ops widens its range after testing against 2.x, or deploy-kit and release-bot move to 3.x after testing.
8545f8cfc0: Uninstall deploy-kit later. The remaining constraint is ^2.0, so the next update may move the dependency to 2.2.x. audit-logger was auto-installed only for deploy-kit. It is now unneeded, and claude plugin prune removes it.
b3d78376d1:
The Java analogy is close but not exact. Maven's nearest-wins mediation would silently pick one version, and the other consumer would fail at runtime with NoSuchMethodError. Gradle's default picks the highest requested version, also silently.

Claude Code's plugin resolver refuses the conflicting install instead. That's closer to npm's peer-dependency errors, or to Gradle with strict version constraints. The trade-off is the usual one: refusing is annoying at install time, and it saves a confusing failure at use time.

On the exam, "the resolver silently picked a version and the plugin broke" is the Maven intuition. It is wrong for this system.
1d42052f5a: Breaking change inside a range. A range trusts the dependency's author to follow semantic versioning. If secrets-vault 2.1.5 renames a tool, ~2.1.0 takes it anyway. Pin exactly (=2.1.4) for dependencies whose authors have broken minors before. Test against the newest in-range tag in your plugin's CI.
21ce503970: Untagged or mis-tagged releases. Range resolution can't see a release whose tag doesn't follow name--vX.Y.Z, or whose plugin.json version disagrees with the tag. claude plugin tag exists to make that check mechanical.
8adaaeabc2: Non-git sources. For npm, archive or command sources, the range is checked at load. It isn't used to choose what is fetched. A mismatch disables the dependent plugin, so the symptom is a plugin that silently goes missing after an update.
61af467d59: Inner packages. Take a plugin pinned at 3.1.0 that starts an MCP server with an unpinned npx package. It is not pinned. The plugin version and every package it runs are separate pins.
622b55819f:
Situation. A 40-developer telecom team runs a ticket-triage service on the Claude API, and uses Claude Code on the same repository. In one week, three things go wrong:

  • (1) On Tuesday afternoon, triage starts sending porting tickets to billing. There has been no deploy since the previous Thursday.
  • (2) A developer's Claude Code session ran kubectl delete against a staging namespace, although CLAUDE.md says not to.
  • (3) A teammate reports that the team's deploy-kit plugin's /deploy-kit:release command fails with "tool not found: secrets_get".

Work each one from the tuple.
df8c4718e6: Triage regression. Pull call records for Monday and Wednesday and diff them (15_repro_tuple.py). model_requested and model_served are unchanged at claude-sonnet-5-5. The prompt version is unchanged at 6, but the sha differs. Someone edited v6 in place through the registry UI to add a billing example. That's two faults: a mutable published version, and an edit that bypassed the gate. Immediate action: restore the v6 content from its recorded hash, or point prod to v5. Fix: make versions immutable in the registry, require the eval gate before any pointer move, and publish the edit as v7 with porting precedence added. The gate then shows its effect on the porting slice before any traffic sees it.
34343280c7: kubectl delete. The rule existed only as text. Add Bash(kubectl delete *) to deny in the committed project settings, plus a PreToolUse hook for context-based checks. Lists merge and deny is evaluated first, so an allow in a developer's local or user file can't override it. If policy says nobody may remove it, even by editing the repo, deploy it in managed settings with disableBypassPermissionsMode.
ec0d186229: Plugin breakage. claude plugin list shows secrets-vault at 3.0.1. deploy-kit declared "secrets-vault" with no range. The vault plugin's 3.0 release renamed its MCP tool to vault_get, and auto-update took it. Fix: publish deploy-kit 3.1.1 with {"name": "secrets-vault", "version": "~2.1.0"}, tag it, and update. Later, test against 3.x and release a version with the new tool name and a widened range.
66ec6d0139: You'd see distractors like these for those stems: "add NEVER DELETE in capitals to CLAUDE.md", "switch triage to Opus", "raise temperature", "ask everyone to reinstall plugins", "turn off auto-update for all plugins forever". Each one treats a configuration-provenance problem as a model problem or a people problem.
06b1abea8c:
The most expensive configuration failures aren't wrong values. They are values that never took effect while everyone believed they had.

Compile errors are loud. Configuration failures in this domain are quiet: a startup warning in a terminal nobody reads, a prompt that never shows in headless mode, a rule that matches no tool. The table collects the quiet paths from the whole chapter, each with the observation that exposes it.
eff23788d6:
The common thread is the gap between declared and effective configuration. Spring developers know it from /actuator/env and /actuator/configprops: the file says one thing, the running application reports another, and only the second counts as evidence.

The habits carry over. Inspect effective configuration in the running tool (/status, /memory, /permissions, claude plugin list). Log the effective tuple in automation. And write CI checks against the gates where values silently stop, not only against file syntax.
37c17c3b35: Permission lists merge across files and are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow. So a personal Bash(*) allow can't override the project's ask or deny. Sending everyone a snippet for user settings relies on compliance. Writing it in CLAUDE.md relies on the model. Managed settings are the answer only if the stem says developers must not be able to change it (they can edit the committed file in a branch).
9cb1401486: From the 4.6 generation on, the model ID is the snapshot, and its weights don't change. Pre-4.6 aliases and Claude Code aliases move; this ID doesn't. Anthropic notes that infrastructure updates can cause minor differences, so per-call logging of the tuple is how you locate a change. Options that propose a date suffix that doesn't exist, or switching providers, are distractors.
b7915f3030: A gate on the mean would ship it. Per-slice thresholds exist for exactly this case. "Ship and monitor" or "canary first" lets users see a regression the offline gate already found. Canary is for regressions that offline evals did not catch.
069c833560: A bare dependency name tracks the marketplace's latest release. A range resolves against tags named name--vX.Y.Z, and auto-update stays within it. Turning off all auto-updates fixes this plugin by freezing everything else too. Copying the other plugin's code in creates a fork to maintain.
5471e2525c: Managed settings sit above command line, local, project and user, and nothing below can override them. Any developer with repo access can edit a committed project file. User settings are personal. A hook in managed settings also can't be removed by a plugin or a project file.
ee8e37c662: Requests to retired models fail, so doing nothing turns into an outage. Switching straight to the replacement in production skips the eval gate. Waiting until the retirement week leaves no time to fix a prompt regression. Export usage from the Console to find the callers nobody listed.
c100011bd2: Allow rules from a project file grant capability, so they wait for trust. Deny and ask rules apply immediately. Some options blame the model, propose adding the rule to CLAUDE.md, or suggest copying the allow into everyone's user settings. They all miss the mechanism. Verify with /status on the joiner's machine.
4f3f07f25e: Model precedence is /model, --model, ANTHROPIC_MODEL, the setting, then ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL. A variable in the CI image is configuration that lives outside the repository. The fix is one reviewed source (the workflow file) plus logging the served model per run. A cost alert alone won't do it.
81b955529a: str.format treats the braces in the JSON example, and in customer text, as placeholders. Escaping braces by hand fixes one template and leaves the next one broken. Editing the published version in place as a hot-fix breaks provenance. The fix ships as a new immutable version.
a4de1e7257: Constraints from all installed plugins must hold, so the fact that ^2.0 alone would choose 2.2.0 is irrelevant. The resolver refuses non-overlapping ranges instead of silently choosing one, unlike Maven nearest-wins mediation. Resolving the conflict is up to a plugin author, who widens or moves a range after testing.
6ff7107585: A shadow exists to measure, so its output is logged and never acted on. Lowering the shadow percentage reduces the duplicates but keeps the defect. Idempotency keys help only where the downstream supports them. Skipping straight to a canary gives up the measurement. Bound the shadow executor and give it its own rate budget, so it can't degrade the serving path.
08b5520981: Making the gate stricter in general doesn't cover cases the dataset lacks. Editing the live prompt text is fast, but it destroys provenance: the per-call log can no longer say what served a conversation. A pointer move restores service in seconds, while the fix ships as a new version through the same gate.
e8cfbcf0aa: In a scratch repo, create .claude/settings.json with the fixed permission block from section 08, plus a .env file. Ask Claude Code to read .env and confirm the deny. Add "Bash(*)" to the allow list in .claude/settings.local.json and confirm git push still prompts. Check /status for the setting sources.
4511b1d1ff: Create a local marketplace with secrets-vault tagged secrets-vault--v2.1.0 and --v3.0.0, and a plugin that depends on it with ~2.1.0. Install it and run claude plugin list to see the resolved version. Then add a second plugin requiring ~3.0 and watch the conflict.
